title: Dyson's bagless prototype: why rebuild it overseas?｜Brand Story
description:
If a bagless prototype already worked, why redevelop it overseas, then return to in-house manufacturing and early British retail orders? Follow factory powder clogging a cloth filter, the diagnosis of a household bag's pores, cardboard and metal prototypes, licensing and joint Japanese development, then tooling finance, rented assembly space, mail-order demonstrations and in-store explanations.

A licensed British Cyclon product existed before Japan; 1983–84 and 550 units come from Dyson's recollection. Italian manufacture applies only to the museum's individual object. Japan is not described as the first market worldwide. The 1985 Nishi-Azabu head-redesign photo, the recalled 1986 agreement with Apex and the Japanese launch are separate records, not grounds for backdating a contract. M+'s 1983/Silver Seiko, V&A's 1986/APEX and the Science Museum Group's 1985–1990/Apex are different collection fields, not one record of a first sale or manufacturing contract.

New material comes from original interview publication pages, the company biography and Robin Roy's interview research. Masters of Scale labels its official transcript as automatically generated and not fully corrected; the author has not separately listened to the audio, and the relevant details still await independent source review. The new bank recollection differs from the older Fortune account in dates and currencies, so the narration uses only the internal appeal and house collateral, without combining them into a precise year and amount. The half-factory interview supplies no location or date and cannot be equated with Bumpers Farm in 1993. The dry-powder demonstration applies the accompanying powder before vacuuming; it is not evidence of wet pickup or a general performance test. The advertising-for-orders deal is another undated recollection of early British distribution, not the same transaction with the first mail-order buyer.

All pictures are anonymous conceptual illustrations; original photographs are used only for research. Original sources, accessed 2026-10-26:

chapters.9m2c: A clogged cloth filter—and an empty bag that still won't suck
chapters.ysz4: A licensee takes it on, but the work continues
chapters.xjwd: A new motor means changes at the inlet too

2566.text: He still faced another question: with famous brands already in the catalogue, why replace them with this unfamiliar product?

9896.text: He bought and fitted a new bag; suction briefly returned, then dropped again.

29pe.text: With just four engineers, who would assemble the new vacuum you needed to deliver?

sthq.text: In the early nineties, Dyson decided to manufacture it himself.

xcms.text: He recalls drawing every component with three engineers, then looking for contractors and toolmakers.

57ap.text: But they found nobody willing to take on the assembly.

qggg.text: I want to know: which troublesome inlet was that perforated cover in Yamamoto's hands originally made for?

t39s.text: And who would persuade a bank to fund the production tooling?

suy4.text: Today, follow Dyson from a bagless prototype to its early acceptance by British retailers.

728h.text: How many people's hands would the bagless idea have to pass through before it became a machine you could sell?

9m2c.text: The principle behind the bagless vacuum in our opening came from a factory problem Dyson had tackled.

4paj.text: The company website dates it to 1978: he was powder-coating metal frames at a factory.

ti4n.text: Much of the powder missed the frames, and extracting the excess clogged a large cloth filter behind them.

8rgv.text: If you needed to keep production running, I'd ask the same thing: what other device could collect that powder?

edty.text: The website also says he saw a large cyclone at a sawmill and wanted to use that separation method at his factory.

zmbc.text: Dyson recalls that an industrial cyclone cost more than they could afford, so they spent several weekends making one themselves.

nzbe.text: He says it was so large that its top had to pass through the roof, requiring a hole in the factory building.

acb6.text: This time, the powder was separated from the air first, rather than relying entirely on the cloth to catch it.

2b6c.text: What interests me isn't its height, but how a blockage led them to a different way of collecting powder.

kdbc.text: Could that method be made small enough for the vacuum in your home?

xmha.text: Dyson says that once, while cleaning at home, the machine indicated a blocked bag, but he had no replacement.

364y.text: So he emptied the bag, taped it shut again and refitted it for a try.

qdgd.text: There was nothing left in the bag, but the machine still wouldn't pick up dirt.

dkhw.text: You might wonder whether a full bag was really the problem. I'd ask what remained after it was emptied.

uj7b.text: He opened it again and saw a coating of fine dust on the inside.

3v4y.text: As he explains it, air had to pass through the bag's pores, but fine dust had blocked those exits.

btuc.text: Earlier, a cyclone had collected powder at the factory. What did he first do at home to test the same idea?

y5py.text: He made a small cyclone from cardboard and tape, then connected it to his existing upright vacuum with a hose.

pd37.text: He replaced the bag with this little model and pushed the machine around to try it.

3yk9.text: That only tested the separation method on an old machine; a complete, saleable product still needed other work.

c8e9.text: Without money for large machine tools, how could he make models to keep changing the shape?

e74a.text: Dyson recalls working at home: unable to afford equipment like a lathe, he used small tools.

xpig.text: He found metal rollers in a second-hand shop, rolled the material into an inverted cone and welded it together.

mcug.text: The tools let him turn the next shape into something real, test it and then decide what to change.

5xeb.text: But if you change several things at once, how do you know which change actually helped?

6nip.text: In another interview, he explains that he changed one thing at a time during prototyping and waited to see the difference.

3b3d.text: It might improve or worsen; understanding what happened would determine the next model.

59xc.text: An Open University interview study also records him making and testing models in brass, aluminium and clear plastic.

5uh4.text: I think that's the key: a model isn't finished just because it's on a shelf. It's a way to resolve an unknown.

azg7.text: Once a working prototype existed, who would pay for tooling and make it in quantity?

ysz4.text: Dyson recalls that he and his partner initially chose to focus on invention, engineering and prototypes.

bjhr.text: Both had manufacturing experience, but this time they wanted a licensed manufacturer to handle production.

2xsw.text: That interview study also identifies tooling expenditure as a hurdle to commercialising this vacuum.

pk83.text: Did anyone actually take a licence and carry out the production?

32ja.text: A licensed British manufacturer did later make the Cyclon.

shcn.text: Dyson dates its production to 1983 and 1984, saying only 550 were made and it was not a commercial success.

xguj.text: One example held by the Science Museum Group is labelled as made in Italy for the British licensee.

jm77.text: So there was a product before Japan. How did Apex find Dyson this time?

kget.text: During this period, the president of Japan's Apex saw a photograph in a design book and contacted Dyson.

ucyp.text: In a later sponsored interview, Yamamoto says it was a book published in the United States in 1984.

pd7s.text: Dyson brought a sample to Japan. The president had wanted to import a finished product, but it wasn't finished.

uih5.text: If you were ordering stock, I imagine you'd ask too: are we taking on a product, or a development project?

hytw.text: In Yamamoto's account, negotiations shifted to remaking it in Japan, with Dyson granting the local sales rights.

upnx.text: Yamamoto says Apex imported stationery and had neither its own engineers nor a factory.

bnk8.text: The president set about finding a factory, while development went to Yamamoto, who had just changed jobs.

iund.text: His studio biography dates his joining Apex to 1985, working on joint development with the British team.

6aj4.text: They found a factory, but had anyone there made this kind of vacuum before?

decj.text: Yamamoto recalls that the manufacturer made precision machinery, rather than specialising in vacuums.

tbv9.text: He himself had never designed a vacuum before, either.

3tsc.text: I think the next challenge was getting these people's work to connect, rather than handing over a sample and waiting for delivery.

u434.text: If you tried to keep the original design, which difference in specifications would stop you first?

xjwd.text: Yamamoto says different British and Japanese voltages meant they had to find another motor.

gnbh.text: They needed a 100-volt motor with similar output, but the one they found was larger.

x6bp.text: To fit it in, they also had to reconsider the casing layout.

5jn4.text: If I were taking on the project, I'd first ask how long this redesign would take to produce a machine we could test.

hq3w.text: In a rough estimate made many years later, Yamamoto put the first Japanese prototype at about six months.

4jy3.text: But once it was assembled, what happened when they pushed it across a carpet?

dzxx.text: He recalls that the motor was very heavy.

w5x9.text: The machine sucked itself against the carpet and was hard to move forward.

dh5b.text: Forcing it forward even cracked the wheels on one occasion.

rs85.text: You might ask what other problems appeared in testing, besides movement.

fphq.text: He also mentions debris blockages and motor overheating that could even melt the casing.

nqdc.text: He estimates that after the first prototype, another year and a half went into fixing problems as they arose.

bteg.text: Yamamoto also points to an inlet inside the bin, with a component he helped design.

4zh9.text: Where did this inlet take the air flowing around the outside?

sby4.text: He describes air swirling around the bin's perimeter, then passing into the cone inside.

88z5.text: Yamamoto says the perforated cover from our opening was fitted at the cone's air inlet to keep debris from blocking it.

mdxt.text: Debris needed to keep circulating outside, while air passed through the inlet towards the centre.

jvsi.text: Once this component was added, what needed adjusting next?

n6tt.text: Yamamoto says they tested different hole sizes and shapes, using those experiments to solve the inlet blockage.

8fq7.text: As the holes changed, the designer at the other end also needed to know how the Japanese tests were progressing.

bgmb.text: When Dyson returned to Britain, how could that design work continue?

qaxx.text: Yamamoto says that when Dyson was in Britain, they repeatedly exchanged faxes.

rvd2.text: Drawings and fax pages shown in the interview preserve records of that collaboration.

a57z.text: You change something at this end, and the other end must follow up. What I see is work going back and forth.

8b48.text: The drawings had to be finished and problems dealt with. Who was responsible under their agreement?

65q8.text: Yamamoto recalls that Dyson was responsible for solving problems and completing the drawings.

6v32.text: Besides faxing, did he come to Japan to work alongside them?

v4g4.text: Yamamoto says Dyson visited Japan several times to get the machine ready for sale.

7q3f.text: Each stay lasted roughly one or two weeks.

3qh9.text: They went to the factory, drew designs and carried out experiments together.

34kb.text: If you want to see what he actually changed, what work does a photograph on the company website preserve?

xw4x.text: Its caption places him in Nishi-Azabu, Tokyo, in 1985, redesigning the head of what became the G-Force.

swdr.text: In a later oral account, Dyson dates the licence agreement with Apex to 1986.

yd8e.text: That and the previous year's redesign are separate records, not a precise contract date we can combine them into.

p8mt.text: Yamamoto's interview also dates the Japanese G-Force launch to 1986.

mgmw.text: Would you expect reaching the shelves to mean huge sales? I want to know how big this business really was.

inii.text: In his 2017 oral account, Dyson calls it a niche product, priced at around 250,000 yen each.

mrr9.text: He says Apex did not achieve great commercial success with the machine.

cx76.text: But the licensing partnership did begin bringing him income.

92cn.text: To reach those component drawings from our opening, he still needed funding and premises for his own manufacturing.

uzwn.text: Once income was coming in, was borrowing for production tooling guaranteed?

jyqr.text: For the tooling funds we asked about at the start, Dyson recalls a visiting bank employee who argued for a loan on his behalf.

4e3p.text: He says the bank first rejected that employee's request, so the employee approached an internal appeals role to seek approval.

ta4q.text: Dyson put his house up as security, and his wife also had to sign the relevant forms.

6w42.text: If you had to pledge the house you lived in, I'd first want to understand which risks fell on me.

7vni.text: Money could buy tooling, but the opening still lacked assemblers. Where would they first find a place to work?

3kk2.text: Those four people found an opportunity with a moulding supplier: half its factory was standing idle.

9qqh.text: He proposed renting that unused half for assembly, avoiding the need to buy an entire factory first.

z8cf.text: But they still had to invest in tooling; renting space didn't remove that expense.

2isp.text: With space secured, who would organise the assembly line, and who would work on it?

g54y.text: He recalls that initially there was no separate production manager or quality-control specialist, just the engineering team.

mdi5.text: The assembly question from the opening finally required hiring a line leader and workers to do the actual assembly.

iv83.text: The company also has a production-line photograph dated 1993. Which site does it show?

i6fq.text: That photograph was taken at Bumpers Farm in Chippenham, Britain.

x8ph.text: Several machines stand along a line, with people working and boxes nearby.

dahx.text: The interview doesn't locate the rented half-factory, so we cannot treat these two records as the same premises.

2wtj.text: But even with machines ready to deliver, were you certain to find retailers willing to stock them?

zi48.text: Dyson remembers a mail-order catalogue buyer first doubting the accompanying dry-powder carpet-cleaning method.

eamp.text: He bought a blackcurrant drink at a petrol station, poured it onto the carpet and then sprinkled on dry-cleaning powder.

cz2v.text: Only then did he vacuum it up. In his recollection, the demonstration worked.

hp4p.text: To be clear, he used the accompanying cleaning powder first; this wasn't a claim that the machine could directly wet-vacuum the drink.

pn7g.text: But why didn't the buyer agree immediately after watching?

b4dg.text: He recalls that the buyer finally agreed to give it a try, becoming the first mail-order catalogue to stock it.

3qra.text: If you were making room in your catalogue, I imagine you'd ask not only whether it could clean, but whether it could sell.

f7dw.text: In another oral account, Dyson says a second mail-order catalogue followed, and then John Lewis.

cm6p.text: Once it reached shops, would retailers also be willing to display the dust users could see?

jtzs.text: A UK Intellectual Property Office decision records him saying that many potential retailers disliked the clear bin.

kiud.text: But he believed customers could see where the dust was, understand how it worked and see the cleaning results.

pwqd.text: According to that testimony, he still chose to keep the transparent design.

vmt8.text: I think the buyer had seen a demonstration, but you, standing in the shop, might not have. Who would explain the difference?

6m9s.text: Dyson recalls having to persuade retailers to put information about the technology and its differences beside the machine.

ng27.text: He wanted buyers to consider performance, durability and use, as well as discounts and prices.

atmg.text: But if a retailer also wanted advertising support and there was no ready budget, how could they negotiate?

cvp5.text: In another recollection of early British retailing, Dyson says an electrical retailer once requested advertising support.

hnrg.text: Without money for advertising at the time, he proposed agreed television advertising tied to the retailer's order volume.

r2i6.text: Dyson says they reached a deal on those terms.

6xye.text: My answer to our opening question is this: the bagless prototype solved part of a blockage problem, but manufacturing and getting retailers to take it still needed people to finish the work.

sptz.text: If you took on this project, which unfinished step would stop you from handing the product over? Tell me in the comments.

5qtc.text: Subscribe to Brand Story to see how everyday products overcome practical obstacles like these.
